candidates.name: inflammation
candidates.definition: When the presence of various inflammatory cell infiltrates occurs together with other prominent morphologic features (congestion, hyperemia, hemorrhage, edema, necrosis, fibrosis, foreign material, bacterial organisms, etc.), it is customary to characterize the change as an inflammation with specific descriptors to further characterize the dominant inflammatory cell type involved.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > inflammatory processes > inflammation

candidates.name: alteration, harderian gland
candidates.definition: In rats, Harderian gland alteration can be observed in the extraorbital lacrimal gland of male and female rats at three months of age, but increases at six month of age only in males. This process appears to be androgen-dependent but also influenced by the absence of estrogen receptors on lacrimal gland acinar epithelial cells in male rats after six months of age (Ferrara et al. 2004). Conversely in mice, females are more frequently affected than males (Krinke 1996). It remains unclear whether this change reflects a metaplastic or a degenerative change. It appears that the Harderian gland cells develop from undifferentiated basal cells of the lacrimal gland acini and intercalated and excretory ducts (Sashima et al. 1989).
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > metaplasia > alteration harderian gland

candidates.name: hepatocellular carcinoma
candidates.definition: A primary malignant tumor arising from hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver, often linked to chronic liver disease such as hepatitis B/C infection, cirrhosis, or aflatoxin exposure. It commonly presents with abdominal discomfort, weight loss, jaundice, and elevated serum alpha‑fetoprotein, reflecting uncontrolled cellular proliferation, angiogenesis, and genetic alterations in pathways like Wnt/β‑catenin and TP53.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > neoplasia > malignant tumor > carcinoma > hepatocellular carcinoma

candidates.name: neoplasia
candidates.definition: Grouping of all morphologies related to neoplasia, which literally means ¿new growth.¿ Neoplastic cells are said to be transformed because they continue to replicate, apparently oblivious to the regulatory influences that control normal cell growth. This is caused by DNA mutations that are (for the most part) acquired spontaneously or induced by environmental insults. These genetic but also epigenetic changes alter the expression or function of key genes that regulate fundamental cellular processes, such as growth, survival, and senescence, resulting in an abnormal growth. (Robbins and Contrand Pathology bases of diseases)
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > neoplasia

candidates.name: necrosis
candidates.definition: Lymphocyte necrosis is characterized by cell swelling with chromatin clumping, karyorrhexis or karyolysis and in more severe lesions, abundant eosinophilic cellular debris. This form of necrosis should be distinguished from apoptosis in which there is individual cell death characterized by cell shrinkage, nuclear pyknosis and fragmentation with apoptotic bodies and tingible body macrophages (lymphocytolysis). S.A. Elmore Toxicol Pathol. 2006; 34(5): 425¿454.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis

candidates.name: single cell necrosis
candidates.definition: single cell necrosis is often interchangeble with apotosis or apoptotic necrosis, as they all are usually represented by individual cells dying of via an apototic process. Apoptosis is a form of genetically controlled 'programmed cell death'. Typical microscopic appearance includes condensed eosinophilic cytoplasm with maintenance of membrane integrity, cytoplasmic budding, nuclear fragmentation in the absence of an inflammatory response.  Diagnosis may be confirmed by electron microscopy, immunostaining (e.g. activated caspase 3) or TUNEL staining. It can occur spontaneously, or be induced by xenobiotics.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > apoptosis necrosis > single cell necrosis

candidates.name: cell injury/death
candidates.definition: grouping of all changes affecting individual or group of cells, characterized by partial or total overwhelminig of the cell capacity to mantain a biochemical and morphological equilibrium, resulting in variuos type of morphologies.

candidates.name: degeneration with necrosis
candidates.definition: in some processes or some specific organs, the degenerative process is always implying some necrosis of the tissue, even if it is not specifically mentioned in the morphology (e.g. retinal degeneration is always accompanied by some necrosis of photoreceptors or other neuronal retinal cells)
candidates.hierarchy: degeneration with necrosis

candidates.name: necrosis, focal/multifocal
candidates.definition: Localized cell death affecting discrete, often scattered, regions of a tissue, rather than a continuous area, typically resulting from ischemia, toxin exposure, or focal inflammation. These focal or multifocal necrotic zones appear as pale, softened spots on gross examination and may be associated with loss of function, pain, or inflammatory infiltrates surrounding the lesions.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis focal multifocal

candidates.name: necrosis, with loss
candidates.definition: Irreversible cell death marked by the breakdown of plasma membranes and intracellular components, leading to the disappearance of the affected tissue or organ’s structural integrity and function. It is typically identified by localized discoloration, swelling, loss of cellular architecture, and subsequent functional deficit in the region where necrosis has occurred.
candidates.hierarchy: necrosis with loss

candidates.name: apoptosis/necrosis
candidates.definition: Necrosis and apoptosis are not always readily distinguishable via routine examination, and the two processes may occur sequentially and/or simultaneously depending on intensity and duration of the noxious agent. This often makes it difficult and impractical to differentiate between both during routine light microscopic examination. In these cases, the combined term apoptosis/necrosis may be used.

candidates.definition: The conventional view of the soft tissues is one of a cellular component comprising fibroblastas, fat containing cells, specialized skeletal muscle fibers, a matrix of ground substance and various structural proteins including collagen and elastic fibers.

candidates.definition: Removal of degenerated/necrotic neurons by phagocytes.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis neuronal

candidates.name: morphologic change

candidates.name: structural alteration
candidates.definition: Grouping of complex morphologic changes implying a combination of inflammatory, reparative, regenerative and/or destructive processes, but also including alteration in the normal development of the tissue/organ. The net effect of these changes is resulting in subgross modifications of the anatomy of the affected tissues, organs or anatomic systems.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > structural alteration

candidates.name: ectopic thymic tissue
candidates.definition: Ectopic and accessory thymic tissue may occur anywhere along the path of descent (thymopharyngeal duct) as the result of failure of descent, sequestration, or failure to involute. they are often observed closed to thyroid/parathyroid but also elsewhere.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > structural alteration > developmental errors > ectopic tissue > ectopic thymic tissue

candidates.name: atrophy, acinar cell
candidates.definition: Acinar cell atrophy can occur focally or diffusely in any exocrine glands. In the pancreas, acinar cell atrophy is the most common spontaneous degenerative change of both rats and mice. Acinar atrophy may range from focal atrophic exocrine acini with no inflammation or fibrosis to diffuse atrophy of exocrine acini with replacement by adipose tissue and residual ducts, vasculature and islets of Langerhans. Acinar atrophy frequently represents the sequel of chronic inflammation and, as such, is often accompanied by infiltrates of mononuclear cells and fibrosis.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > atrophy > atrophy epithelial > atrophy acinar cell

candidates.name: atrophy, ductal
candidates.definition: Generalized or segmental narrowing of ductal lumina with normal appearing epithelium, or slightly lower epithelial height. In the epididymis, it is generally caused by decreased androgen support or decreased fluid and sperm output from the testis.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > atrophy > atrophy ductal

candidates.definition: Decrease of acinar cell zymogen granules (degranulation) or mucin leading to shrunken acinar cells. It can occur in any lymph node and there can be differences in the presence and severity of lymphoid depletion between lymph nodes in the same animal. Lymphoid depletion is typically characterized by a decrease in the number and size of follicles with few to no germinal centers and/or depletion of paracortical lymphocytes. With a depletion of paracortical lymphocytes, the stromal cells may become more prominent. (S.A. Elmore Toxicol Pathol. 2006; 34(5): 425¿454)

candidates.definition: The leakage of blood from ruptured or permeable vessels into the surrounding interstitial space characterizes extravasation of blood in a tissue. It results from trauma, inflammation, or vascular pathology, leading to localized swelling, discoloration (ecchymosis or petechiae), pain, and impaired perfusion as erythrocytes and plasma accumulate outside the vascular lumen, triggering inflammatory and coagulation cascades.

candidates.name: extravasation of blood
candidates.definition: The leakage of blood from damaged vessels into surrounding tissues, often due to trauma, inflammation, or vascular fragility, constitutes extravasation of blood. It manifests as bruising, swelling, hematoma formation, or discoloration, reflecting the accumulation of erythrocytes outside the circulatory system and the subsequent inflammatory response.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > hemodynamic disorders > extravasation of blood

candidates.name: microhemorrhages
candidates.definition: Microhemorrhages are very small hemorrhages, with only few erythrocytes entering the extravascular space.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > hemodynamic disorders > extravasation of blood > hemorrhage > microhemorrhages

candidates.name: extravasation of blood in a cavity
candidates.sanitized_name: extravasation of blood in a cavity
candidates.definition: Leakage of blood from damaged vessels into a body cavity, such as the pleural, peritoneal, or cranial space, resulting in accumulation of liquid blood within that compartment. It is typically indicated by sudden pain, distension, decreased organ function, and imaging or aspirate findings that reveal non‑clotted blood without external bleeding, reflecting disruption of vascular integrity and subsequent hematoma formation in the cavity.
candidates.hierarchy: extravasation of blood in a cavity

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > hemodynamic disorders > extravasation of blood > hemorrhage agonal

However in certain parenchymas or conditions, the differentiation of the two processes is not possible, and some pathologists prefer to mention the processes as combined in one morphology.

candidates.definition: Affected cells may show increased cytoplasmic granularity, cell swelling, and eosinophilia. candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > cytoplasmic alteration

candidates.definition: epithelial vacuolation is characterized by fine to coarse vacuolation of the cells, often secondary to subtle damage to the epithelial cells. candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation epithelial

candidates.definition: The presence of abnormal, often lipid‑ or protein‑rich vacuoles within the cytoplasm of endocrine cells, reflecting cellular injury, metabolic stress, or secretory dysfunction. candidates.name: vacuolation, biliary epithelium

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration vacuolar > swelling intracellular organelles

candidates.name: vacuolation, tubular
candidates.definition:
Occasional solitary vacuoles can be seen as an incidental finding in most control testes. This diagnosis should only be used when the number of vacuoles is above control levels. Vacuolation is generally an early morphological indicator of disturbance to the Sertoli cell. The vacuoles may be intracellular or intercellular and in both cases probably reflect a disturbance in fluid balance of the Sertoli cell. Microvacuolation of the
basal Sertoli cell cytoplasm occurs with some Sertoli cell toxicants and with some phospholipidosis-inducing chemicals. Significant germ cell degeneration and necrosis are often accompanied by vacuolation of the tubular epithelium, secondary to the loss of the space occupying germ cell from between the Sertoli cell processes. Tubular vacuolation should only be used as a diagnosis when the vacuolation is considered
a primary or separate event
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation tubular

candidates.name: vacuolation, lipidic (fatty change)
candidates.definition: Hepatocellular vacuolation is usally lipidic in nature, nevertheless, vacuoles may develop from increased intracellular fluid contents within vesicles and/or by swelling of cytoplasmic organelles; it is usually divided into two main types, namely, microvesicular and macrovesicular named according to the size of vacuoles, although mixed forms can frequently be observed. The nature of the change therefore needs often a further characterization via special stains (Oil red O or Sudan Black on cryostat sections can demonstrate fat /EM can detect organelle swelling). Fatty change is accepted as a diagnosis only for liver. Fatty change can also be observed in combination with other hepatotoxic injuries (e.g., chronic liver toxicity, degeneration, inflammation, and necrosis) or nutritional disturbance (e.g. diet, vitamin A excess) in both animals and man.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation lipidic > vacuolation lipidic

candidates.name: vacuolation, tubular epithelium
candidates.definition: Accumulation of clear, membrane‑bound vacuoles within the cytoplasm of renal tubular epithelial cells, often reflecting cellular injury, metabolic disturbance, or toxic exposure. This histopathologic change is seen as swollen, pale‑appearing tubules on microscopy and may accompany impaired reabsorption, proteinuria, or acute kidney injury.
candidates.hierarchy: vacuolation tubular epithelium

candidates.name: vacuolation, tubular epithelium (fatty droplets)
candidates.definition: Accumulation of lipid‑rich vacuoles within the cytoplasm of renal tubular epithelial cells, visible as clear, round spaces that replace normal eosinophilic staining. This histologic change reflects intracellular fat deposition due to metabolic disturbances (e.g., obesity, diabetes, ischemia) or toxic injury, and may be associated with tubular dysfunction, proteinuria, and impaired renal concentrating ability.
candidates.hierarchy: vacuolation tubular epithelium

candidates.name: vacuolation, tubular
candidates.definition:
Occasional solitary vacuoles can be seen as an incidental finding in most control testes. This diagnosis should only be used when the number of vacuoles is above control levels. Vacuolation is generally an early morphological indicator of disturbance to the Sertoli cell. The vacuoles may be intracellular or intercellular and in both cases probably reflect a disturbance in fluid balance of the Sertoli cell. Microvacuolation of the
basal Sertoli cell cytoplasm occurs with some Sertoli cell toxicants and with some phospholipidosis-inducing chemicals. Significant germ cell degeneration and necrosis are often accompanied by vacuolation of the tubular epithelium, secondary to the loss of the space occupying germ cell from between the Sertoli cell processes. Tubular vacuolation should only be used as a diagnosis when the vacuolation is considered
a primary or separate event
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation tubular

candidates.name: vacuolation
candidates.definition: Accumulation of substances of different character, including fluids, lipids, phospholipids, and glycoproteins within cells. They usually appear as round structures in the cytoplasm, with empty or pale eosinophilic contents. Special techniques are necessary to further characterise the nature of those structures and to differentiate the content.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation

candidates.name: vacuolation, epithelial
candidates.definition: epithelial vacuolation is characterized by fine to coarse vacuolation of the cells, often secondary to subtle damage to the epithelial cells. A slightly different type of vacuolation can be seen when amphiphilic cationic drugs are given to rodents. Such drugs can cause intralysosomal storage of polar phospholipids in various organs
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation epithelial

candidates.name: cytoplasmic alteration
candidates.definition: Affected cells may show increased cytoplasmic granularity, cell swelling, and eosinophilia. Hepatocellular granularity may be due to swelling of cell organelles or increase in the numbers of cell organelles including peroxisomes, mitochondria, and smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > cytoplasmic alteration

candidates.name: vacuolation, glandular epithelium
candidates.definition:
Vacuolation of epithelial cells in glands due to accumulation of substances of different character,
including fluids, , lipids, phospholipids, and glycoproteins
within cells.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation epithelial > vacuolation glandular epithelium

candidates.name: vacuolation, lipidic (fatty change)
candidates.definition: Hepatocellular vacuolation is usally lipidic in nature, nevertheless, vacuoles may develop from increased intracellular fluid contents within vesicles and/or by swelling of cytoplasmic organelles; it is usually divided into two main types, namely, microvesicular and macrovesicular named according to the size of vacuoles, although mixed forms can frequently be observed. The nature of the change therefore needs often a further characterization via special stains (Oil red O or Sudan Black on cryostat sections can demonstrate fat /EM can detect organelle swelling). Fatty change is accepted as a diagnosis only for liver. Fatty change can also be observed in combination with other hepatotoxic injuries (e.g., chronic liver toxicity, degeneration, inflammation, and necrosis) or nutritional disturbance (e.g. diet, vitamin A excess) in both animals and man.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation lipidic > vacuolation lipidic

candidates.name: vacuolation, squamous epithelium
candidates.definition: Accumulation of clear, membrane‑bound vacuoles within the cytoplasm of squamous epithelial cells, often reflecting cellular injury, metabolic disturbance, or toxic exposure. This histopathologic change may be associated with epithelial thinning, loss of barrier function, and can be observed in inflammatory, infectious, or drug‑induced lesions.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation epithelial > vacuolation squamous epithelium

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation lipidic

candidates.name: necrosis, olfactory epithelium
candidates.definition: Loss of cellular integrity in the olfactory epithelium results from irreversible injury that leads to the death of the specialized sensory and supporting cells lining the nasal cavity, often triggered by toxic inhalants, infection, ischemia, or severe inflammation. This necrotic process manifests as diminished or absent sense of smell, nasal discharge, and may be accompanied by ulceration or crusting of the nasal mucosa.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis epithelial > necrosis olfactory epithelium

candidates.name: degeneration, epithelial
candidates.definition: Degeneration of an epithelium is caused by cellular dysfunction and may lead to breakdown of the epithelial barrier and inflammation/inflammatory cell infiltrate. Degeneration can take specific morphologies according tot he type of epithelium, e.g. the degeneration of respiratory epithelium is often characterized by loss of cilia, cytoplasmic blebbing, and picknosis of nuclei. At the ending of the airway tree, the loss of normal apical blebs from Clara cells are typical early degenerative lesions seen with particulates, while compounds requiring metabolisc can induce degeneration and necrosis of clara cells. In other epithelia, the degeneration is usually associated with variable alteration in staining properties, intracellular vacuolation or extracellular edema (spongiosis), and often admixed with numerous necrotic cells.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration epithelial

candidates.name: vesicle, cornea

candidates.name: atrophy
candidates.definition: Atrophy is the loss of cell substance resulting in the cell shrinkage in the size. When a sufficient number of cells are involved, the entire tissue or organ diminishes in size, becoming atrophic. Although atrophic cells may have diminished function, they are not dead.Causes of atrophy include a decreased workload, loss of innervation, diminished blood supply, inadequate nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, and aging (senile atrophy).
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > atrophy

candidates.name: decreased, bone mass (trabeculae)
candidates.definition: A reduction in the quantity and connectivity of the trabecular bone network, leading to thinner, more widely spaced trabeculae and loss of structural integrity. This condition manifests as lowered bone mineral density, increased fragility, and a higher risk of fractures, often resulting from imbalanced remodeling where osteoclastic resorption outpaces osteoblastic formation due to aging, hormonal changes, nutritional deficiencies, or chronic disease.
candidates.hierarchy: decreased bone mass

candidates.name: aplasia
candidates.definition: aplasia and agenesis are terms used synomously. They describe the absence of an anatomic part of an organ or the entire organ itself due to a congenital, developmental disorder. This is often not a histopathological lesion, but rather an anatomic abnormality observed grossly. It is a congenital, developmental absence of tissue.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > structural alteration > developmental errors > malformation > aplasia

candidates.name: lymphoid tissue, present
candidates.definition: Aggregates of lymph tissue in submucosal or perivascular position can be frequently observed and represent the formation of lymphoid follicle. They represent immunological active stations to protect the body from possibly harmful agents, such as the MALT (M. F. Cesta Toxicol Pathol 2006 34: 599)
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > immunomodulation > steady state of the immune system > lymphoid tissue present

candidates.name: atrophy, lymphoid
candidates.definition: Lymphoid depletion or atrophy is the sequela to chronic necrosis or apoptosis. It can occur in any lymph node and there can be differences in the presence and severity of lymphoid depletion between lymph nodes in the same animal. Lymphoid depletion is typically characterized by a decrease in the number and size of follicles with few to no germinal centers and/or depletion of paracortical lymphocytes. With a depletion of paracortical lymphocytes, the stromal cells may become more prominent. (S.A. Elmore Toxicol Pathol. 2006; 34(5): 425¿454)
candidates.hierarchy: atrophy lymphoid

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > structural alteration > organ specific entities changes > glomerular changes > glomerulonephritis

candidates.name: glomerular injury
candidates.definition: Chronic inflammatory/degenerative change in the glomeruli and marked hemodynamic alterations with basement membrane thickening with/without immune complex deposition and/or mesangial cell proliferation and/or lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration. Glomerulonephritis and glomerulopathy are very similar processes, although in the former the exudative process tends to be dominant, in the latter the degenerative process is more evident.

candidates.definition: The alteration of immune system activity—either enhancement or suppression of specific immune responses—to maintain physiological balance or achieve a therapeutic effect. candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia

candidates.definition: Cardiomyopathy is a degenerative change characterized by myocyte degeneration/necrosis, an increase in the amount of interstitial fibrous connective tissue, and in some cases mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltration.

candidates.name: mature fibrosis
candidates.definition: A stage of fibrotic tissue remodeling marked by dense, highly cross‑linked collagen deposition, markedly reduced cellularity, and loss of normal extracellular‑matrix organization, resulting in irreversible scarring. Clinically it presents as stiff, non‑compliant tissue that impairs organ function (e.g., decreased lung compliance, hepatic cirrhosis) and is associated with persistent inflammation and myofibroblast activation.
candidates.hierarchy: mature fibrosis

candidates.name: myocardiofiber degenerationreplacement by fibrosis
candidates.definition: Cardiomyopathy is a degenerative change characterized by myocyte degeneration/necrosis, an increase in the amount of interstitial fibrous connective tissue, and in some cases mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltration.

candidates.name: immature fibrosis
candidates.definition: A provisional, loosely organized deposition of extracellular matrix components—primarily collagen—that has not yet undergone full cross‑linking or remodeling, typically observed in the early stages of tissue repair or chronic injury. It is characterized by a cellular infiltrate of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, minimal tensile strength, and histologic features such as fine, non‑eosinophilic fibers, indicating ongoing fibrogenesis before mature scar formation.
candidates.hierarchy: immature fibrosis

candidates.name: pulmonary fibrosis
candidates.definition: The critical event in the pathogenesis of pulmonary fibrosis is generally considered to be the release of potentially fibrogenic cytokines and fibronectin from macrophages activated as part of the inflammatory response to injury of lung parenchyma. Pulmonary fibrosis in laboratory rats is most frequently observed as part of a chronic inflammatory response to repeated injury to the lung parenchyma. However, severe acute lung injury from a single exposure may induce a relatively rapid fibrogenic response that may or may not be reversible. The term fibrogenesis has been used to describe potentially reversible fibroblast proliferation and minimal cross-linking of protein, as compared to true pulmonary fibrosis, in which extensive cross-linking has occurred and lesions are not reversible.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > healing and repair > fibrosis > pulmonary fibrosis

This is caused by DNA mutations that are (for the most part) acquired spontaneously or induced by environmental insults. These genetic but also epigenetic changes alter the expression or function of key genes that regulate fundamental cellular processes, such as growth, survival, and senescence, resulting in an abnormal growth. (Robbins and Contrand Pathology bases of diseases)

It manifests as lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and heightened immune activity, and is observed in infections, autoimmune disorders, or malignancies.

candidates.definition: Proliferation of lymphohemopoietic cells, malignant

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > normal altered physiological condition > altered physiological condition > altered estrous cycle > absence corpus luteum

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > normal altered physiological condition > altered physiological condition > altered estrous cycle > decreased number absent corpora lutea

candidates.name: necrosis, hepatocellular
candidates.definition: Usually present as single of multiple foci of necrotic hepatocytes, may be accompanied by inflammatory cells, but always with a random parenchymal localization or subcapsularly, due to hypoxic change secondary to impaired blood flow. candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular

candidates.name: necrosis, focal/multifocal
candidates.definition: Localized cell death affecting discrete, often scattered, regions of a tissue, rather than a continuous area, typically resulting from ischemia, toxin exposure, or focal inflammation. These focal or multifocal necrotic zones appear as pale, softened spots on gross examination and may be associated with loss of function, pain, or inflammatory infiltrates surrounding the lesions.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis focal multifocal

candidates.name: necrosis, zonal
candidates.definition: Necrosis in a parcticular zone of the liver lobule (Centrilobular, Midzonal, Periportal, Diffuse) secondary to direct or indirect damage from xenobiotic exposure or tissue anoxia.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular > necrosis zonal

candidates.name: necrosis, zonal, centrilobular
candidates.definition: Necrosis of the hepatocytes adjacent to /in the area of the central vein. Sometimes referred to as periacinar necrosis.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular > necrosis zonal > necrosis zonal centrilobular

candidates.name: necrosis
candidates.definition: Lymphocyte necrosis is characterized by cell swelling with chromatin clumping, karyorrhexis or karyolysis and in more severe lesions, abundant eosinophilic cellular debris. This form of necrosis should be distinguished from apoptosis in which there is individual cell death characterized by cell shrinkage, nuclear pyknosis and fragmentation with apoptotic bodies and tingible body macrophages (lymphocytolysis). S.A. Elmore Toxicol Pathol. 2006; 34(5): 425¿454.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis

candidates.name: necrosis, zonal, diffus
candidates.definition: A pattern of cell death characterized by diffuse, zone‑specific loss of viable tissue, typically observed in organs such as liver or kidney where necrosis spans entire lobular or cortical zones without a sharp border. It results from widespread metabolic, ischemic, or toxic injury, leading to uniform cytoplasmic eosinophilia, nuclear fading, and organ dysfunction manifested by elevated enzymes and clinical signs of failure.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular > necrosis zonal > necrosis zonal diffus

candidates.name: necrosis, zonal, periportal

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular > necrosis zonal > necrosis zonal periportal

candidates.name: necrosis, zonal, midzonal
candidates.definition: Necrotic (eosinophilic) liver cells intermediate to the central vein and the portal triad. This necrosis is the least common form of zonal necrosis and is mediated by specific toxicants.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular > necrosis zonal > necrosis zonal midzonal

candidates.name: necrosis, hepatocellular
candidates.definition: Usually present as single of multiple foci of necrotic hepatocytes, may be accompanied by inflammatory cells, but always with a random parenchymal localization or subcapsularly, due to hypoxic change secondary to impaired blood flow. Subcapsular necrosis has also been reported from direct pressure secondary to gastric distention and from some types of restraint.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular

candidates.name: necrosis, zonal, centrilobular
candidates.definition: Necrosis of the hepatocytes adjacent to /in the area of the central vein. Sometimes referred to as periacinar necrosis.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis hepatocellular > necrosis zonal > necrosis zonal centrilobular

candidates.name: cell injury/death
candidates.definition: grouping of all changes affecting individual or group of cells, characterized by partial or total overwhelminig of the cell capacity to mantain a biochemical and morphological equilibrium, resulting in variuos type of morphologies.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death

candidates.name: hepatoblastoma
candidates.definition:
Hepatoblastomas consist of organoid structures often oriented around vascular spaces. They are usually seen with other types
of hepatocellular tumors, especially within hepatocellular adenomas. Rare reports of this lesion in rats appear in literature.
They are seen in certain strains of mice and have also been induced by certain hepatocarcinogens.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > neoplasia > malignant tumor > hepatoblastoma

candidates.name: hepatocellular carcinoma
candidates.definition: A primary malignant tumor arising from hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver, often linked to chronic liver disease such as hepatitis B/C infection, cirrhosis, or aflatoxin exposure. It commonly presents with abdominal discomfort, weight loss, jaundice, and elevated serum alpha‑fetoprotein, reflecting uncontrolled cellular proliferation, angiogenesis, and genetic alterations in pathways like Wnt/β‑catenin and TP53.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > neoplasia > malignant tumor > carcinoma > hepatocellular carcinoma

candidates.name: neoplasia
candidates.definition: Grouping of all morphologies related to neoplasia, which literally means ¿new growth.¿ Neoplastic cells are said to be transformed because they continue to replicate, apparently oblivious to the regulatory influences that control normal cell growth. This is caused by DNA mutations that are (for the most part) acquired spontaneously or induced by environmental insults. These genetic but also epigenetic changes alter the expression or function of key genes that regulate fundamental cellular processes, such as growth, survival, and senescence, resulting in an abnormal growth. (Robbins and Contrand Pathology bases of diseases)
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > neoplasia

candidates.name: carcinoma, embryonal
candidates.definition: Proliferation of testicular epithelium (germ cells), malignant (testicular germ cell tumours).  In the females, the tumors are derived from the anlage of the Müllerian ducts show a biphasic pattern and can exhibit both epithelial and mesenchymal characteristics.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > neoplasia > malignant tumor > carcinoma > carcinoma embryonal

candidates.name: degeneration, tubule
candidates.definition: degeneration encompasses several morphologic changes in renal epithelial cells associated with loss of viability including tinctorial change, vacuolation, blebbing, cellular sloughing and other alterations including repair. When a particular component(i.e. vacuolation) is much more prominent or the even the exclusive type of change noted, then one of these more specificmorphologic diagnoses can be utilized instead of the more general term of degeneration.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration tubule

candidates.name: degeneration, tubular
candidates.definition:
Degeneration tubular is from the male repro manuscript ¿Diagnostic features (may include any combination of the following 1. candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration tubular

candidates.name: degeneration, epithelial
candidates.definition: Degeneration of an epithelium is caused by cellular dysfunction and may lead to breakdown of the epithelial barrier and inflammation/inflammatory cell infiltrate. Degeneration can take specific morphologies according tot he type of epithelium, e.g. the degeneration of respiratory epithelium is often characterized by loss of cilia, cytoplasmic blebbing, and picknosis of nuclei. At the ending of the airway tree, the loss of normal apical blebs from Clara cells are typical early degenerative lesions seen with particulates, while compounds requiring metabolisc can induce degeneration and necrosis of clara cells. In other epithelia, the degeneration is usually associated with variable alteration in staining properties, intracellular vacuolation or extracellular edema (spongiosis), and often admixed with numerous necrotic cells.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration epithelial

candidates.name: degeneration/atrophy, tubular
candidates.definition: Diagnostic features: 1.Some tubules depleted of all germ cells and lined only by Sertoli cells. 2. Some tubules with partial germ cell depletion 3.  Some tubules containing actively degenerating or apoptotic germ cells 4. A mixture of the features described for ¿¿degeneration, tubular¿¿ and ¿¿atrophy, tubular¿¿.  It is highly recommended that ¿¿degeneration/atrophy, tubular¿¿ be used as the summative diagnosis when there are combinations of changes that include atrophy, degeneration, vacuolation, exfoliation, and so on. This is preferred over listing individual diagnoses. In most cases of tubular degeneration/atrophy, there will be a proportion of tubules that are undergoing active germ cell degeneration (tubular degeneration) and a proportion of tubules that have lost all of their germ cells (tubular atrophy).¿
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration atrophy tubular

candidates.name: atrophy, tubule
candidates.definition: INHAND term atrophy, tubular (ID 6279) mapped as a synonym to this term.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > atrophy > atrophy epithelial > atrophy tubule

candidates.name: degeneration, ductular/alveolar epithelium
candidates.definition: Loss of structural integrity and functional capacity of the bronchiolar ductular and alveolar epithelial cells, characterized by cellular atrophy, vacuolization, detachment, and impaired gas exchange, often accompanied by inflammation, fibrosis, and reduced pulmonary compliance. Clinically it manifests as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration ductular alveolar epithelium

candidates.name: degeneration, ductular/sebaceous epithelium

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration ductular sebaceous epithelium

candidates.name: vacuolation, tubular epithelium (fatty droplets)
candidates.definition: Accumulation of lipid‑rich vacuoles within the cytoplasm of renal tubular epithelial cells, visible as clear, round spaces that replace normal eosinophilic staining. This histologic change reflects intracellular fat deposition due to metabolic disturbances (e.g., obesity, diabetes, ischemia) or toxic injury, and may be associated with tubular dysfunction, proteinuria, and impaired renal concentrating ability.
candidates.hierarchy: vacuolation tubular epithelium

candidates.name: vacuolation, tubular epithelium
candidates.definition: Accumulation of clear, membrane‑bound vacuoles within the cytoplasm of renal tubular epithelial cells, often reflecting cellular injury, metabolic disturbance, or toxic exposure. This histopathologic change is seen as swollen, pale‑appearing tubules on microscopy and may accompany impaired reabsorption, proteinuria, or acute kidney injury.
candidates.hierarchy: vacuolation tubular epithelium

candidates.name: necrosis, renal tubules
candidates.definition: A pathological process in which the epithelial cells lining the renal tubules undergo irreversible cell death, often triggered by ischemia, nephrotoxic agents, or severe inflammation. It manifests as acute tubular injury with loss of brush‑border integrity, tubular dilation, cast formation, and clinically presents as oliguria, rising serum creatinine, and impaired renal concentrating ability.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis renal tubules

candidates.name: foamy macrophages
candidates.definition: all macrophages with foamy appearance, irrespective of the location, have been mapped together into the same child term. They may belong to alveolar macrophage aggregates or other-tissue macrophage aggregates, therefore both relationships have been created.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > deposition accumulation > compartmental cell accumulation > macrophage aggregates > foamy macrophages

candidates.name: inflammatory cell infiltrate, perivascular
candidates.definition: Infiltrates of inflammatory cells in a perivascular stroma expanded by edema, hemorrhage, congestion, and/or proliferating fibroblasts (fibroplasia).
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > inflammatory processes > infiltrate inflammatory cell > inflammatory cell infiltrate perivascular

candidates.name: inflammation, vascular/perivascular
candidates.definition: The use of the two terms (vasculitis and vasculopathy) have been historically discouraged in toxicological pathology, as their use, in association with the vessel and/or the anatomical region affected, may inherently imply a similarity to specific human conditions, which is often not the case. In line with this, all these terms have been mapped under the morphological descriptor "vascular/perivascular inflammation"
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > inflammatory processes > inflammation > inflammation vascular perivascular

candidates.name: accumulation, mixed inflammatory cells, around blood vessels
candidates.sanitized_name: accumulation mixed inflammatory cells around blood vessels
candidates.definition: A perivascular accumulation of various leukocytes (lymphocytes/macrophages/ neutrophils) seen as background changes as well as in infectious, inflammatory, or autoimmune diseases; therefore check the report for the toxicological relevance of them
candidates.hierarchy: accumulation mixed inflammatory cells around blood vessels

candidates.name: vacuolation, macrophage
candidates.definition: macrophages, due to their scavenger activity, are prone to display vacuolation of their cytoplasm. These vacuoles can be due to the accumulation of phagocytized material into the lysosomal compartment. The origin of the material can vary according to the location of macrophages, the test material dosed in the experiment. Not last, they may also represent part of a generalized phospholipidogenic process.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation macrophage

candidates.name: macrophage aggregates
candidates.definition: Clusters of macrophages that accumulate in tissues, forming nodular or plaque‑like structures in response to chronic inflammation, infection, or persistent foreign material. Their presence is identified histologically by densely packed macrophage cells—often containing lipids, pigments, or fibrotic debris—and is commonly associated with granulomatous lesions, tissue remodeling, and impaired clearance of pathogens or debris.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > deposition accumulation > compartmental cell accumulation > macrophage aggregates

candidates.definition: Abnormal amount of mature trabecullar bone  (also called cancellous or spongy bone)  consisting of delicate bars and sheets of bone, trabeculae, which branch and intersect to form a sponge like network.
candidates.hierarchy: increased mature trabecular bone

candidates.name: morphologic change
candidates.definition: A morphologic change is any structural alterations of cells and tissues at microscopic level, assessed by comparison with similar unaffected tissues, by the meaningfullness of the variation from the expected pre-existing condition and/or not last by the experience of the pathologist describing the change.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change

candidates.name: increased, bone mass (trabeculaae)
candidates.definition: An elevation in the amount of trabecular bone tissue, reflected by higher trabecular thickness, number, or connectivity, resulting in greater overall bone mass within the spongy interior of skeletal elements. This phenotype often arises from enhanced osteoblast activity, reduced osteoclast‑mediated resorption, or genetic/ hormonal factors (e.g., estrogen excess, Wnt pathway activation) and may be detected by imaging as denser, more robust trabecular architecture.
candidates.hierarchy: increased bone mass

candidates.sanitized_name: decreased bone trabeculae and or cortex
candidates.definition: decreased bone results from an imbalance in bone formation and resorption, with relative reduction in the bone. It can be spontaneous (age-related), due to immobilized/disuesd limb, or generalized (associated with cortisonme toxicity, thyrotoxicosis, dextran sulfate etc)
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > structural alteration > abnormal growth differentiation > abnormal bone modelling remodelling > decreased bone trabeculae and or cortex

candidates.name: hyperplasia, glandular
candidates.definition:
Glandular hyperplasia is characterized
by an increased number of active proliferating
glands. Proliferation is obvious and reflected in an
increased number of mitotic figures.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia glandular

candidates.name: hyperplasia, respiratory epithelium
candidates.definition: increased layers of surface respiratory epithelial cells, often forming protusion. In the larynx epithelial hyperplasia has higher tendency to form small fronds of epithelium, usually without cilia
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia epithelial cell > hyperplasia respiratory epithelium

candidates.name: hyperplasia, mucosa
candidates.definition: Hyperplasia of the mucosa is a reactive or regenerative process and often follows injury due to chemicals, infectious agents and irradiation.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia epithelial cell > hyperplasia mucosa

candidates.name: hyperplasia, mucous cell
candidates.definition: mucus cells are usually pinpointing the respiratory epithelium and they are variably present at different levels of the airways.  Hyperplasia refers to the replacement of respiratory epithelium by mucous cells either as a single layer or as a pseudostratified layer, in areas where mucous cells are normally present
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia epithelial cell > hyperplasia mucosa > hyperplasia mucous cell

candidates.name: hyperplasia, mucosal, with hypertrophy
candidates.definition: Mucosal hyperplasia in a hollow organ is characterized by an increased thickness of the mucosa
candidates.hierarchy: hyperplasia mucosal with hypertrophy

candidates.name: hyperplasia, VNO
candidates.definition: An abnormal increase in the number of cells within the vomeronasal organ (VNO), resulting in epithelial thickening and often accompanied by inflammation or mucus accumulation. This proliferative response can impair chemosensory signaling, leading to reduced pheromone detection and may be associated with nasal discharge, irritation, or secondary infections.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia epithelial cell > hyperplasia vno

candidates.name: hyperplasia, olfactory epithelium
candidates.definition: this lesion is characterized by an increased thickness of the epithelium resulting from an increase in the number of sustentacular, olfactory sensory precursors and/or basal cells
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia epithelial cell > hyperplasia olfactory epithelium

candidates.name: hyperplasia, exocrine cell
candidates.definition: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in an organ or tissue, usually resulting in increased mass of the organ or tissue.
candidates.hierarchy: hyperplasia exocrine cell

candidates.name: hyperplasia, mucosal, regenerative
candidates.definition: Regeneration takes place by replication of mature mucosa cells which appear basophilic.
candidates.hierarchy: hyperplasia mucosal regenerative

candidates.name: hyperplasia, focal, mucosa (glandular stomach)
candidates.definition:
Focal or multifocal  proliferative changes of the the gastric mucosa. No significant compression of adjacent tissue. Proliferation may be manifested as an increase in mucosal
thickness or penetration of glands through the muscularis mucosae to the submucosa, tunica muscularis, or serosa forming cystic or glandular diverticula.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia epithelial cell > hyperplasia mucosa > hyperplasia focal mucosa

candidates.name: vacuolation
candidates.definition: Accumulation of substances of different character, including fluids, lipids, phospholipids, and glycoproteins within cells. They usually appear as round structures in the cytoplasm, with empty or pale eosinophilic contents. Special techniques are necessary to further characterise the nature of those structures and to differentiate the content.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation

candidates.name: swelling, intracellular organelles
candidates.definition: Retention of fluid and/or metabolic by-products leading to cell swelling
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration vacuolar > swelling intracellular organelles

candidates.name: degeneration, vacuolar
candidates.definition: This term has a long historical usage in pathology, however it has not been contemplated in any of the existing INHAND manuscripts, therefore it is kept to guide the mapping, however the usage may decrease over time.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration vacuolar

candidates.name: vacuolation, cortical, increased, diffuse
candidates.definition: Diffuse microvesicular vacuolation is a normal pattern in the adrenal cortex. In some strains there is a slight difference between genders. A variety of xenobiotics can increase lipid deposition and macrovacuolar vacuolation in the adrenal cortex usually by inhibition of steroid synthesis, however it may represent a degenerative process. Small, foamy and optically clear vesicles (microvesicular) or large vacuoles (macrovesicular) in cytoplasm of cortical cells can be observed, and the cells may be enlarged and/or the number of cortical cells may be increased. Cellular enlargement caused primarily by the accumulation of lipid is diagnosed as vacuolation and not hypertrophy.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation endocrine cell > vacuolation cortical increased diffuse

candidates.name: vacuolation, cortical, decreased, diffuse
candidates.definition: Diffuse lipid depletion in cortical cells, due to degeneration or physiological response of cortical cells. The cytoplasm is more dense and homogeneous eosinophilic than usual with a reduction in lipid vacuole. Decreased vacuolation may represent a result of ACTH-induced lipid depletion, stress or administration of xenobiotics. Cortical cells are normal in size. It the cortical cells are increased in size then they should be considered hypertrophied. Chronic stress or conditions that significantly increase serum ACTH concentrations would also be expected to induce diffuse cortical hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > degeneration > degeneration endocrine cell > vacuolation cortical decreased diffuse

candidates.name: vacuolation, cortical, increased, focal
candidates.definition: Focal increased vacuolation is a common, spontaneous change in aged rats. It is usually characterized by discrete, well demarcated increased cytoplasmic vacuolation of cortical cells with gradual transition to the surrounding cortex at the periphery.It usually occurs in one or more zones of the cortex, such as the zona fasciculata or glomerulosa. Individual cells may be increased in size, but the number of cells within the lesion is not increased. Slight to marked compression and increase in size beyond the regular cortical thickness may occur when combined with degenerative changes such as sinusoid dilatation and cystic degeneration.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation endocrine cell > vacuolation cortical increased focal

candidates.name: vacuolation, epithelial
candidates.definition: epithelial vacuolation is characterized by fine to coarse vacuolation of the cells, often secondary to subtle damage to the epithelial cells. A slightly different type of vacuolation can be seen when amphiphilic cationic drugs are given to rodents. Such drugs can cause intralysosomal storage of polar phospholipids in various organs
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation epithelial

candidates.name: vacuolation, tubular
candidates.definition:
Occasional solitary vacuoles can be seen as an incidental finding in most control testes. This diagnosis should only be used when the number of vacuoles is above control levels. Vacuolation is generally an early morphological indicator of disturbance to the Sertoli cell. The vacuoles may be intracellular or intercellular and in both cases probably reflect a disturbance in fluid balance of the Sertoli cell. Microvacuolation of the
basal Sertoli cell cytoplasm occurs with some Sertoli cell toxicants and with some phospholipidosis-inducing chemicals. Significant germ cell degeneration and necrosis are often accompanied by vacuolation of the tubular epithelium, secondary to the loss of the space occupying germ cell from between the Sertoli cell processes. Tubular vacuolation should only be used as a diagnosis when the vacuolation is considered
a primary or separate event
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation tubular

candidates.name: vacuolation, theca cell
candidates.definition: Increased or decreased vacuolation in theca cells may be associated with alterations of steroid synthesis or phospholipidosis.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation endocrine cell > vacuolation theca cell

candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > metabolic derangement > vacuolation > vacuolation lipidic

candidates.name: necrosis, testicular
candidates.definition: Irreversible death of testicular tissue resulting from ischemia, infection, trauma, or torsion, which disrupts spermatogenesis and androgen production. It manifests as acute scrotal pain, swelling, discoloration, and may be confirmed by imaging or histopathologic evidence of cellular breakdown.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cell injury death > necrosis > necrosis testicular

candidates.name: reduced, spermatogenesis
candidates.definition: A decrease in the generation of spermatozoa within the seminiferous epithelium, leading to lower sperm counts (oligospermia) or absence of sperm (azoospermia) and often reduced testicular volume. It results from disruptions in germ cell proliferation, meiosis, or hormonal regulation and may be caused by genetic defects, endocrine disorders, toxic exposures, or testicular injury.

candidates.name: pigment
candidates.definition: Pigmentation in most tissues consists of lipofuscin and/or hemosiderin, usually present in interstitial macrophages. Nevertheless other cells are capable of accumulating pigments (e.g. hepatocytes, renal tubular cells). Pigments may also originate from specific compounds or their metabolites. Special stains and/or other investigations are necessary to further characterize the origin of the pigments in a given tissue.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > deposition accumulation > intracellular accumulation > accumulation endogenous material > pigment

Age-associated intracellular accumulation of cell degradation products;lipofuscin represents residual bodies derived from autophagosomal lysosomes and is composed of polymers of lipid and phospholipid
complexed with protein.
candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > deposition accumulation > intracellular accumulation > accumulation endogenous material > pigment > lipofuscin accumulation

candidates.definition: A macrophage aggregate is an accumulation of macrophages, mimicking a granuloma-like lesion but usually not associated with any other inflammatory cells or epitheloid macrophages/giant cells. candidates.hierarchy: morphologic change > cell adaptation injury death > cellular adaptation of growth > hyperplasia > hyperplasia gallbladder

candidates.name: dilatation, glandular
candidates.definition: An abnormal widening or expansion of a gland’s ductal or acinar structures, typically arising from obstruction, inflammation, hormonal imbalance, or tissue degeneration, which increases gland size and may alter its secretory output. Clinically it presents as localized swelling, discomfort, and changes in the volume or composition of the gland’s product (e.g., saliva, mucus, or hormonal secretions).

candidates.definition: Regeneration of tubular epithelium following necrosis/exfoliation where the basement membrane remains intact. this is the preferred INHAND term for regenerating tubular epithelium, which is often resistant to the initial nephrotoxin, because effects such as diminished secretory carrier systems or loss of the brush border may prevent further accumulation of toxin. However, completely regenerated tubules may again be susceptible resulting in cyclic waves of degeneration and regeneration. In such cases, degeneration/regeneration as combined diagnoses has been used. In the absence of any other evidence of regeneration or degeneration, tubular basophilia is the preferred term.

candidates.definition: Restoration of damaged or lost epithelial cells through coordinated proliferation, migration, and differentiation that re‑establishes tissue architecture and barrier function. candidates.definition: in the kidney, tubule hyperplasia is characterized by an increase in the number of tubule lining cells but not intraluminally or beyond a single layer. simple tubule hyperplasia can be spontanous as in CPN or can be chemically induced and may be a consequence of single cell degneration with compensatory regeneration.

candidates.name: infarction
candidates.definition: A localized area of tissue necrosis resulting from the abrupt cessation of arterial blood flow, which deprives cells of oxygen and nutrients. Clinically it manifests as sudden pain, loss of function, and possible organ‑specific signs (e.g., chest pain in myocardial infarction) due to ischemic injury and subsequent cell death.
candidates.hierarchy: infarction

candidates.name: infarct, acute
candidates.definition: Acute infarcts have occurred very recently and are characterized by necrosis of the tissue and possible fibrinous exudate. They can be poorly defined and slightly hemorrhagic, so called red infarcts. Red infarcts are located in tissues with dual circulations (e.g., lung, small intestine). White infarcts occur with arterial occlusions in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (e.g., heart, spleen, kidney).
candidates.hierarchy: infarct acute

candidates.name: infarct, chronic
candidates.definition: A chronic infarct is a permanently damaged area of tissue that resulted from prolonged ischemia and has persisted for weeks to months, leading to necrosis, scar formation, and fibrosis. It manifests as lasting functional loss or organ‑specific symptoms (e.g., chronic chest pain, reduced contractility, or neurologic deficits) and is characterized histologically by collagen deposition, loss of viable cells, and remodeling of the affected region.
candidates.hierarchy: infarct chronic

candidates.definition: Grouping of all morphologies related to neoplasia, which literally means ¿new growth.¿ Neoplastic cells are said to be transformed because they continue to replicate, apparently oblivious to the regulatory influences that control normal cell growth. These genetic but also epigenetic changes alter the expression or function of key genes that regulate fundamental cellular processes, such as growth, survival, and senescence, resulting in an abnormal growth.
